Tower defence is not listed. The data is older (2017), but the gradient is consistent with Sensor Tower's 2026 finding that men dominate strategy and women dominate puzzle.

findings.claim: Quantic Foundry's current model defines a 'calm' and 'cozy' pole of player preference. It describes pausable, predictable, low-stimulation play with no weapons or gore.
findings.evidence: The Gamer Motivation Model v3 reference sheet (2M+ gamers) defines low Excitement as Calm: turn-based or pausable, relaxed, predictable, low visual stimulation. Low Destruction is defined as Cozy: enduring familiarity, no weapons or gore, typically G/PG. The Mastery-Achievement cluster is described as cool-headed, long-term play that makes plans and watches cities or farms grow.

findings.claim: On mobile in 2025, strategy and puzzle were the two fastest-growing revenue genres and hybridcasual was the only segment with meaningful in-app purchase growth. The casual audience is older than PC/console and skews female in puzzle.
findings.evidence: Sensor Tower State of Gaming 2026 (summarised by GameDev Reports): mobile strategy made $20.2B and puzzle $14.4B, the 'strongest growth'. Hybridcasual in-app revenue grew +20% YoY, and top hybridcasual titles have overtaken the top-25 casual games on D7 retention. 60% of casual/hypercasual players are over 35. Women make up a larger share in puzzle, lifestyle and casino; men dominate strategy, sports and shooters.

findings.claim: Sort, screw and block hybridcasual puzzles are the fastest-growing part of an otherwise flat casual market. However, the space is crowded and saturated.
findings.evidence: AppMagic H1 2026 (via GameDev Reports): casual in-app revenue was about $11B, flat. Puzzle made $4.9B, including hybridcasual puzzles at about $600M. Sort-puzzle revenue rose +229% YoY and downloads +56%. More than 2,000 block puzzles launched in H1'26 (+89% YoY). Match-3 made $2.5B, flat. Merge-2 made $1.3B (+74%). Gamigion adds that none of 120 new Match-3 releases passed $100K per month.

findings.claim: Screw and sort puzzles were already growing fast in 2025, while strategy led overall mobile in-app revenue.
findings.evidence: Mobilegamer.biz data digest: AppMagic data shows screw-puzzle revenue reached $27M in Q1 2025, almost 4x the same quarter a year earlier. Wool Sort passed 4M downloads, and Rollic's Screw Jam leads the subgenre's in-app revenue. Sensor Tower Q4 2024 data shows strategy had the highest in-app revenue at $4.8B (+27% YoY).

findings.claim: Sort and jam hybridcasual puzzles now sit among the top-grossing US puzzle games next to established brands.
findings.evidence: Sensor Tower's Q4 2025 US top-5 puzzle games by revenue are Pixel Flow! (above $2M, 457K downloads), NYT Games, Magic Sort! (about $1.4M, 958K+ active users), Color Block Jam (Rollic, $1.3-1.7M) and June's Journey.

findings.claim: The top-grossing mobile tower defence games are midcore, combat or gacha titles. None of them target the cozy or puzzle audience.
findings.evidence: Sensor Tower's Q2 2025 US Android top-5 tower defence games: Arknights (peak about $527K per week), Kingdom Guard: Tower Defense (about $192K per week), Watcher of Realms (about $155K per week), Raid Rush TD ($75-85K per week) and Galaxy Defense: Fortress TD (about $102K per week, launched April 2025). All five use war, fantasy-combat or sci-fi themes.

findings.claim: 'Cozy' has become a major commercial positioning on Steam. Surveyed players say they play to de-stress and at their own pace, and few want challenge.
findings.evidence: A GameDiscoverCo analysis (reported by Outlook Respawn) found that the share of $100K+ revenue Steam games describing themselves as 'cozy' rose from 0.4% in 2022 to 3.1% in 2025 (+675%). Sago's 2025 omnibus survey (US, UK, FR, ES, DE) found 53% play to switch off from stress, 52% value playing at their own pace, and 51% say it calms them and improves their mood. Only 10-17% cite challenge as a draw.

findings.claim: Cozy tower defence is thinly supplied, mostly on PC, and has no strong mobile or portrait entrant.
findings.evidence: The itch.io 'cozy' + 'tower defense' tag lists 78 results, and none of the top 10 mention mobile or portrait play. Dampf - The Cozy Tower Defense (Steam, March 2024) has only 13 reviews (76% positive); its core cozy feature is that the player decides when the next wave starts. CozyWorld's September 2026 list of cozy tower defence games can only name about six titles, mostly on PC, plus the ageing Plants vs. Zombies.

findings.claim: Accessible, low-time-commitment tower defence and strategy hybrids can sell well to casual players.
findings.evidence: Thronefall, a minimalist strategy/tower defence game by a two-person studio, was designed for time-constrained, casual-accessible play. It sold just under 1M copies in about a year, was released on iOS in June 2025, and its IP was acquired by Mythwright in December 2025.

findings.claim: Older US players are a large, mobile-first puzzle audience that plays to keep their minds sharp and to relax. Boomer women out-play Boomer men.
findings.evidence: ESA 2026: 212.3M Americans play weekly, the average age is 37, 80% play on mobile, and puzzle is the top mobile genre (66%). Adults cite stress relief (78%) and mental stimulation (79%). Kotaku's coverage of ESA 2026: 84% of Boomer and Silent Generation players regularly play on mobile, 74% play puzzle games, and 32% of people aged 81-90 play. ESA 2025: older players' motivations are relaxing or passing time (77%) and keeping minds sharp (65%). 52% of Boomer women play versus 46-47% of Boomer men.

findings.claim: Matching and puzzle audiences are about three-quarters women and mostly over 35. Players over 50 are the most engaged per day.
findings.evidence: Udonis compiled Facebook Gaming, GameAnalytics and App Annie data: women are 75% of US matching-puzzle and word players, 74% in the UK, 66% in Japan and 73% in South Korea. The majority are 35+, and players over 50 spend the most daily time (about 17.6 minutes). This is a secondary compilation of 2021-22 data.

findings.claim: US parents are broadly positive about games and often play with their children. They also actively restrict which game types their children can play.
findings.evidence: Marist Poll (June 2025, n=876 parents of children under 18): 48% say games are mostly positive and 15% mostly negative. 65% restrict game types and 66% set time limits. Top concerns are online safety (20%), lack of physical activity (18%), screen time (15%) and violent or inappropriate content (13%). 27% play with their children daily and 38% weekly. ESA 2025: 82% of parents who game play with their kids, 52% weekly, and 70% prefer their kids play games rather than use social media.

findings.claim: Parents object to in-game spending and gambling-like mechanics such as loot boxes.
findings.evidence: A Ygam/Mumsnet survey of more than 1,000 UK parents of 7-17 year-olds: 78% are concerned about screen time, 35% say their child spends money on in-game purchases, and 52% have seen gambling-style mechanics such as loot boxes in their child's games.

findings.claim: Young children's gaming time has jumped, and most of it happens on phones and tablets. Ages 5-8 are a large mobile-gaming cohort.
findings.evidence: Common Sense Census 2025 (2024 data): children aged 0-8 average 38 minutes of gaming per day, up 65% since 2020, of which 21 minutes is on smartphones or tablets. Ages 5-8 average 1 hour 4 minutes per day, 34 minutes of it on smartphones or tablets. 51% of children 8 and under have their own mobile device.

findings.claim: Bloons TD 6 is non-violent, but parent guides flag its in-app purchases and note it can be too complex for younger children. This leaves room for a family and co-play tower defence game.
findings.evidence: Zift's parent guide lists Bloons TD 6 as rated 9+, $4.99 upfront with in-app purchases from $0.99 to $17.99, and advises parents to password-protect purchases. It says the fast-paced, complex play may confuse younger children and suits older kids better.

findings.claim: iOS returns on ad spend are much stronger than Android's for casual games, and strategy and kids games perform especially well on iOS.
findings.evidence: Liftoff/Singular 2025 Casual Gaming Apps Report: average D30 return on ad spend (ROAS) for casual games is 47% on iOS versus 15% on Android. On iOS, sports reaches 80%, kids 68% and strategy 60% (Android: 21%, 8% and 27%). Some genres have about 10x higher cost per install on iOS. Roughly 50% of casual installs come from ads shown in hypercasual and puzzle games.

findings.claim: Phones are mostly used portrait and often one-handed, and mobile game sessions are short and frequent.
findings.evidence: Hoober/UXmatters field study (1,333 observations, 2013, older but foundational): 49% of users hold the phone one-handed, 36% cradle it and 15% use two hands. 67% of one-handed users touch with the right thumb, and 90% of two-handed use is in portrait. GameAnalytics 2025 benchmarks (cited by Udonis): the median mobile session is 5-6 minutes (8-9 minutes in top games), with about 4 app opens per day.

findings.claim: Royal Match shows that polish, simplicity and a season pass can win the adult casual puzzle audience without complex meta-systems.
findings.evidence: Naavik deep dive: Royal Match succeeded by obsessing over simplicity, a smooth board and no loading screens, and dropped the decoration layer. Its Royal Pass (June 2021) is estimated to have added +31% revenue and Endless Treasure +20%. It charges the highest extra-move prices in the genre, and events are always overlapping. Revenue per download doubled year on year.

findings.claim: Games built around 'satisfying' ASMR-style feedback have been a long-running mobile trend, and relaxing casual sims can still break out.
findings.evidence: Apptopia (2021, dated): the number of mobile games with 'ASMR' in their title or description rose for 13 straight quarters, reaching 405 in Q2 2021 (+72.3% YoY). All top-10 ASMR titles were hypercasual; for example, Sushi Roll 3D had 14.3M downloads in Q2 2021. A 2025 example: Insightrackr reports the cooking sim Cookingdom passed 10M downloads in April 2025 (+1,200% month on month, #9 by downloads), monetising mainly through ads.

implications: Target niche: adult puzzle players aged 30-55, mostly women, including lapsed strategy fans whose attention is now shorter. They play sort and jam puzzles to 'keep their mind sharp' and relax, but avoid tower defence because every top-grossing tower defence game is war- or gacha-themed and male-skewed. Parents who co-play with 6-10 year-olds, and 50+ mobile puzzle players, are secondary audiences reached by the same design choices. Research showed no strong portrait-mode, mobile, cozy tower defence game.

The central twist should borrow the most satisfying verb in the fastest-growing puzzle subgenre (sorting, matching or routing by colour) and make it the in-wave tower defence decision. Example: during a wave, the player flips path switches or gates so colour-coded creatures reach the matching tower. This gives short-horizon, few-parameter decisions every few seconds, which fits Quantic Foundry's finding that strategy appeal has declined. Tower placement and upgrades supply the long-term planning.

Make the game non-violent and non-adversarial. Enemies should be messes, pests or sleepy creatures that get sorted, tidied, washed or tucked in rather than killed; players 'win' by protecting a nurturing goal, similar to a cultural victory in 4X. This makes it Quantic Foundry's 'cozy' pole, suits all ages, and reaches both women and older players, who prefer non-confrontational wins.

Build in the 'calm' pole: pause at any time, let the player start the next wave, offer a speed toggle, keep enemy behaviour predictable, and add a no-fail or relaxed mode. Also offer a harder optional mode, because some audiences vary widely in how much strategy they want.

Design for portrait and one thumb: tappable targets at the bottom of the screen, big hit areas, and a vertically winding path. Keep each wave to 30-90 seconds and each level to 3-6 minutes so a level fits a 5-6 minute median session, with a mid-level save.

Treat ASMR and 'satisfying' feedback as core design: pops, squishes, snaps when a colour set is completed, chains of combos, and a tidy board after each wave. Every signal must also be readable with sound muted, using colour plus shape, which also covers colour-blind players and older eyes.

Monetisation should fit a family and adult-women audience and avoid loot boxes and gambling-style mechanics (52% of UK parents have seen them and object). Recommended model: free first world, then a one-time 'full game' unlock or premium level packs, cosmetic tower and creature skins, and an optional season or 'garden pass' with visible rewards. Offer ads only as opt-in rewarded ads, or remove them entirely for a kids-safe build. iOS D30 ROAS is 60% for strategy and 68% for kids casual games, which supports an iOS-first launch.

Market it as a satisfying puzzle-defence game, not as 'strategy', because women and older players under-index on strategy as a label. App Store creatives should show the sort/route twist in the first 3 seconds, as sort and jam puzzle ads do, since about half of casual installs come from ads in puzzle and hypercasual games.

Risk: hybridcasual puzzles are saturated (more than 2,000 block puzzles launched in H1 2026, and none of 120 new Match-3 games passed $100K per month). The differentiator must be real tower defence depth: tower synergies, upgrade paths and replayable strategies. The game must not reduce to another sort level with a tower defence skin.

Retention hooks to prototype: a daily 'tidy challenge' with a fixed seed, star or mastery goals per level to satisfy Completion motivation, a collectable creature journal to satisfy Completion and Design, and cosmetic customisation of the garden or home to satisfy Design, which women over-index on.

niches.audience: Adults who play sort, jam and colour puzzles (roughly 30-55, mostly women, iPhone-first). They play to relax and to 'keep the mind sharp', but have never tried tower defence.
niches.why_underserved: Every top-grossing US tower defence game (TD) has a combat, war or gacha theme: Arknights, Kingdom Guard, Watcher of Realms, Raid Rush and Galaxy Defense. Nothing in the genre is pitched at these players. Meanwhile their own genre is filling with shallow clones: more than 2,000 block puzzles launched in H1 2026, and none of 120 new Match-3 games passed $100K a month. Routing by colour and shape, with fixed rules, is a verb they already know, and real TD depth would set a game apart from those clones. Critical caveat: this audience is used to free-to-play (F2P) games with ads, 3-minute levels and hybridcasual monetisation. A free-to-try premium TD will convert only a fraction of them. Treat them as the group that widens reach and marketing, not as the core payers. That sort-puzzle players will cross over to TD is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
niches.size_signal: Pixel Flow! made $105M from in-app purchases (IAP) in about 10 months, and Color Block Jam $148M. Sort-puzzle revenue grew 229% year on year (AppMagic, H1 2026). Puzzle is the top mobile genre in the US at 66% (ESA 2026). About 75% of US matching-puzzle players are women, and most are over 35.

niches.audience: Time-poor and lapsed adult strategy players (roughly 25-45) who 'like the idea of strategy more than the reality' and want deep but short sessions on a phone.
niches.why_underserved: The minimal one-twist TD hybrids these players buy are almost all PC-only: Thronefall (about 1M), The King is Watching (500K+) and 9 Kings (400K in its first month). Only Thronefall has reached iOS (June 2025). BTD6 rounds often run past 30 minutes, and Kingdom Rush is the only mobile reference for 10-15 minute missions. Quantic Foundry shows strategy appetite shifting toward shorter planning horizons. Strategy appeal holds steady with age while appetite for competition drops sharply, so single-player, non-PvP decisions with short horizons suit this group. Caveat: they are proven payers on Steam, but nobody has measured how well they convert on iOS. Their absence from iOS may partly reflect developers doubting iOS returns.
niches.size_signal: Thronefall sold 315K units in 2 months and about 1M in a year. The King is Watching passed 500K by March 2026. Quantic Foundry: the average Strategy motivation fell from the 50th to the 33rd percentile between 2015 and 2024.

niches.audience: Cozy, calm players who want low-stress, non-violent strategy they can pause and play at their own pace.
niches.why_underserved: Cozy TD is scarce and mostly on PC. itch.io lists 78 cozy + TD results with no mobile or portrait focus, a September 2026 list can name only about 6 titles, and the one commercial example, Dampf, has just 13 reviews. Honest caveat: thin supply may signal weak demand as much as opportunity. Only 10-17% of cozy players cite challenge as a draw, which clashes with TD's fail states. Serve them through the theme (enemies are cheered up, not killed), pause anywhere, player-started waves and a Relaxed mode, but do not make them the only target.
niches.size_signal: The share of $100K+ Steam games calling themselves 'cozy' rose from 0.4% in 2022 to 3.1% in 2025. In Sago's 2025 survey, 53% play to switch off from stress and 52% value playing at their own pace. In 4X games, women are 3x more likely than men to pursue non-military victories.

niches.audience: Parents who play with 6-10 year-olds, and players over 50 who want non-violent, mentally stimulating games without loot boxes.
niches.why_underserved: BTD6 is non-violent, but parent guides flag its in-app purchases and say it is complex for younger children. The hybridcasual puzzles these households play are ad-heavy, and 52% of UK parents have seen loot-box mechanics in their child's games and object to them. A model with no ads, no currency and directly priced cosmetics, plus colour-and-shape readability, serves them without a separate build. Caveat: targeting under-13s directly brings in Kids Category rules, and local co-op is out of scope for the slice. Treat them as a secondary audience reached through design choices, not a marketing target.
niches.size_signal: 27% of US parents play games with their children daily and 38% weekly (Marist 2025). Children aged 5-8 average 34 minutes a day of phone and tablet gaming. 84% of Boomer and older players play on mobile, and 74% play puzzle games (ESA 2026).

niches.audience: Lapsed or fatigued BTD6 and Kingdom Rush players who find the meta solved and want more to do during a wave.
niches.why_underserved: Veterans say every BTD6 mode except CHIMPS is trivial and that builds repeat. Runs of 100+ rounds cause burnout, and the game cannot be paused mid-wave to act. In-wave agency is mostly ability buttons, and the only live-reroute feature is a gimmick on a single map (the Workshop map's Track Extensions). A TD whose core in-wave verb is routing gives them new decisions without leaving the genre. Caveat: they judge against 26 towers and 70+ maps, so the slice must prove depth per tower and replayable combinations. They are a smaller, harsher audience.
niches.size_signal: BTD6 was still #2 US iOS paid game in Q3 2025, with about 200K active users (Sensor Tower estimate). It had 1.1M daily active users in 2021 (MTG). 97% of its 230K Steam reviews are positive.

twists.name: Live junction gates that sort a mixed stream of enemies into kill zones (the candidate evaluated in depth)
twists.novelty:
High within TD. No shipped, notable TD makes live junction switching its core loop:
- BTD6 has it only as a 20-second gizmo on one map.
- Mazing games fix the route once a wave starts (TDS developer: the path is already calculated).
- ChangePath is an itch.io demo with no reviews.
- Train Towers steers your own train, not the enemies.
The verb itself is proven in adjacent hits: Conduct THIS! (Apple Editors' Choice), Anomaly (iOS Metacritic 94, Apple Design Award), Railbound (Apple Design Award for Interaction) and Mini Metro (about 6M sales). Colour sorting is the hottest mobile puzzle verb (Pixel Flow, $105M). It is simple to explain ('tap a gate, steer the colours') and gives the strongest 3-second App Store or video hook of the six candidates.
twists.risks:
1. Lock-and-key: if each colour maps to exactly one tower and resists everything else, the game becomes a sort puzzle with a TD skin and one right answer per enemy. Doucet warns against this. Use soft counters (roughly 1.5x damage against the favoured family, 0.6x against the disfavoured one) so misrouting is costly but not fatal.
2. Frantic tapping: Conduct THIS! was widely called too hard. Start with one gate, allow planning while paused, send enemies in groups, and use a per-gate cooldown of about 1s rather than a fee per flip. A fee taxes the core verb; it suits a gimmick like the Workshop map, not a primary mechanic.
3. The twist and the towers crowding each other out: towers can become secondary, or gates can become pointless once towers are strong. Tune so routing quality changes the outcome at every stage, and give late waves new routing problems, not just more hit points.
4. Solvability: fixed rules can produce one best sequence, which hurts replay. Mixed groups, zones that fill up and several workable tower-to-lane assignments keep more than one solution.
5. Late-wave tap overload: sell limited gate automation as an upgrade, like Rail Route's sensors, so tapping stays manageable. Keep manual override so the twist never disappears.
6. Map constraint: branching channels need portrait space. Keep 2-3 gates and 3-4 channels on one screen.
7. Positioning: it could read as a kids' sort game to strategy players. Test the art direction with both groups.

twists.name: Attention lens (drag a spotlight that strengthens the towers under it)
twists.in_wave_decisions: Where to park or sweep a limited focus that raises fire rate or unlocks a tower's special attack while watched, and when to leave a zone unattended.
twists.novelty: Medium. This is essentially The King is Watching's 'gaze' (500K+ copies, though that game is a kingdom builder, not TD) applied to TD. BTD6's area buffs and ability buttons already cover part of the same ground.
twists.risks: On a phone the finger covers the zone being boosted, the same occlusion complaint BTD6 players already raise about tower placement. It tends toward a degenerate 'park it on the chokepoint' strategy. Steam-literate players would see it as derivative. Continuous dragging suits two hands, not one-thumb portrait play. It is weak as a still screenshot.

twists.name: Live path drawing (lay and re-lay a limited supply of track tiles mid-wave)
twists.in_wave_decisions: Where to extend or cut the route while enemies are moving, spending a limited tile budget between lengthening their exposure and protecting a zone.
twists.novelty: Medium-high. Mazing is mature but done before or between waves (Desktop TD, Fieldrunners, and Emberward's 'build a maze before the battle begins'). Mini Motorways proves real-time route drawing works, but without combat.
twists.risks: The hardest candidate to polish in a slice: pathfinding edge cases, exploitable mazes, drag precision and finger occlusion on a 375px screen. A route that changes shape is harder to read at a glance than a flipped gate. Emberward (97% positive) and Rogue Tower already own the path-building flavour, and Isle of Arrows players complained about randomness and having no undo.

twists.name: Mid-wave redeploy (lift a tower and drop it on another pad after a short downtime)
twists.in_wave_decisions: Which tower to pull from a quiet zone to reinforce a busy one, accepting that it stops firing while it moves.
twists.novelty: Low-medium. Arknights has built its play around redeploying units mid-wave at huge scale ($678M lifetime revenue). Unstoppable Gorg's rotating orbit is the premium precedent.
twists.risks: Closely associated with Arknights and gacha games. Dragging competes with the placement gesture, and the style rewards heavy micro-management, which tires casual and cozy players. It is less legible in a 3-second clip, and relocation risks dissolving placement strategy, which is TD's main planning layer.

twists.name: Rhythm-synced towers (tap on the beat to power up volleys; each tower adds a music layer)
twists.in_wave_decisions: When to spend taps powering up a tower in time with the beat.
twists.novelty: Medium, but commercially unproven. The Rhythm Towers demo has 14 reviews and the full game has no release date. Bass Defense is obscure.
twists.risks: Fails the brief's requirement to read clearly with sound off, and many phone players play muted. It creates accessibility problems for hearing-impaired players and those without a strong sense of rhythm, and it turns decisions into timing execution rather than strategy. Better used as flavour: tune tower hits and pops to a musical scale.

twists.name: Tower retuning (tap a tower to cycle its colour or ammo to match incoming enemies)
twists.in_wave_decisions: Which towers to retune for the next group of enemies, given a short delay each time.
twists.novelty: Low-medium. Colour-resistance TD already exists (Color Tower Defence, 13 reviews), as do colour-queue archers (Rainbow Rush) and conveyor-ammo colour matching (Color Guard).
twists.risks: It is the same colour-matching decision as sorting, but without the spatial flow, so it is less satisfying to watch and harder to read: many small tower states instead of a few large gates. It pushes hard toward lock-and-key counters, and its tap targets are many small towers rather than a few big gates, which is worse for one-thumb portrait play.

synthesis.recommended_concept:
RECOMMENDATION: a portrait, one-thumb 'puzzle-defence' game with a working title such as 'Gloom & Bloom' (the name needs a trademark check).

AUDIENCE
- Primary: adults who like the idea of strategy but bounce off war/gacha TD and 30-minute BTD6 rounds. This is where niche 1 (sort-puzzle players) and niche 2 (time-poor, lapsed strategy players) overlap.
- Served on the side through the theme and the monetisation model: cozy players and families.
- Kept engaged through a hard 'Flow' mode: BTD6 veterans.
- Market it as a satisfying puzzle-defence game rather than 'strategy', because women and older players under-index on strategy as a label.

THEME
- Setting: a canal garden lit by lanterns at dusk.
- Enemies: grumpy little rain-cloud creatures ('Mopes') drift down a winding canal toward a sleeping village's lily pond.
- Towers: garden keepers cheer them up with chimes, bells and mist.
- Defeat: each cheered Mope bursts into a bloom in its family's colour (petals, fireflies, paper lanterns). The blooms settle on the banks, so the drab canal visibly flowers over the course of the level. This progress is visible and makes a shareable end-of-level picture.
- Losses: each enemy that gets through wilts a lily in the pond, so lives are something you can see.
- Why this theme:
  - It is non-violent, which suits the 3x preference for non-military wins among women and older players, and the concerns parents raise.
  - It suits ASMR audio: water, wooden gate clacks and chimes tuned to a pentatonic scale.
  - It looks nothing like the war and gacha art that dominates the grossing chart.
- Art direction: prefer a refined paper-cut or risograph look with a dusk palette over saccharine cuteness, so adult strategy players do not dismiss it as a kids' game. Apple Design Award winners reward charm and craft, not graphical fidelity.

THE ONE TWIST
- Tapping a wooden sluice gate at a junction flips it live, steering each group of Mopes into the channel whose towers suit it.
- Three enemy families, each with its own shape, colour and behaviour, e.g. blue drop = fast, amber block = armoured, magenta star = splits into two when cheered.
- Towers are soft counters, not immunities.
- Constraints that make gate flipping a decision rather than a reflex:
  - a per-gate cooldown of about 1s;
  - enemies arrive in mixed groups;
  - channels differ in length;
  - kill zones fill up and saturate;
  - later enemies jam a gate or split at it.
- Some tower pads sit where channels run close together, so one tower can cover two lanes. This ties placement to routing.
- Gate upgrades (faster swing, one auto-sort rule) compete with towers for money, which keeps tapping manageable as waves get denser.

WHY THIS TWIST, JUDGED AGAINST THE OTHERS
- It is the only candidate that is genuinely open in shipped TD: the BTD6 Workshop gimmick is on one map only, mazing games fix the route once a wave starts, and ChangePath is an unreviewed demo.
- Its verb is proven on iPhone: Conduct THIS!, Anomaly, Railbound and Mini Metro.
- It borrows the fastest-growing puzzle verb, sorting.
- It uses discrete taps, so there are no drag-precision or finger-occlusion problems. The lens and path-drawing twists fail here.
- It stays readable muted through gate arrows, water flow and lane tints. The rhythm twist fails here.
- It sells in a 3-second App Store clip.
- It targets the genre's main criticism ('more watching than doing') and BTD6 pain points: no mid-wave action and solved builds.

Critically, the junction twist wins only if it is built with soft counters and throughput pressure. As a pure colour-to-tower match, it collapses into another sort puzzle in a saturated market.

SLICE SCOPE
- Length: one level of about 20 waves, 12-15 minutes, with an autosave after every wave.
- Towers: four (a fast single-target tower, a heavy tower that cracks armour, a splash-and-slow mist tower, and a long-range support tower).
  - Each has 2 upgrade paths of 3 tiers.
  - Only one path can reach tier 3.
- Enemies: 6-7 types, including a boss that splits at gates.
- Map: 2-3 gates and 3-4 channels on one portrait screen.
- Time controls: pause any time, with gate flipping allowed while paused in Standard mode, plus 1x and 2x speed.
- Modes:
  - Standard.
  - Flow: hard, with no flipping while paused and no auto-sort.
  - Relaxed.
- Gate dock: a row of buttons in the bottom thumb zone mirrors every gate, showing its direction and icons for the next arrivals.

KILL CRITERIA FOR THE PROTOTYPE
Rework the constraints before adding content if any of these happen:
- players do not use gates unprompted by wave 3;
- wins depend on towers alone;
- routing becomes a single forced answer;
- testers describe it as frantic.

Unverified assumptions:
- that sort-puzzle players will cross over to TD;
- how well free-to-try converts on iOS.

Test both before committing to an iOS build.
synthesis.monetisation_plan:
MODEL: free to try, then a one-time unlock
- The free download includes:
  - the first waterway: the browser-slice level plus 2-3 short intro levels;
  - all four towers and all upgrade paths within that waterway;
  - no ads.
- A single non-consumable 'Full Garden' unlock costs $6.99 (test $5.99-7.99). It opens:
  - all launch waterways;
  - Flow (challenge) mode;
  - the daily seeded challenge;
  - Relaxed mode.
- The unlock screen lists exactly what the purchase adds, as Guideline 3.1.1 requires for trial-style offers.
- Rationale:
  - BTD6 ($6.99, 4.9 stars from 348K ratings) and Balatro ($9.99, #2 US paid in 2025) show that paying $7-10 once is accepted.
  - Paid apps get only about 4% of mobile downloads.
  - Isle of Arrows ($5.99, 272 ratings) shows how little reach a paid-only indie TD gets.
  - Thronefall's iOS port is free to try.
  - No verified conversion data exists for free-plus-unlock games, so measure it in soft launch.

AFTER THE UNLOCK: optional spending, never power
1. Waterway expansions at $4.99-9.99 every 4-6 months.
   - Each adds a new junction mechanic (turntable, one-way valve, timed lock), 1-2 enemy families and a free playable preview level.
   - Ship them only when stable: Rogue Legends sits at 45% positive after a buggy launch and a charge of rushed paid releases.
   - Use regional pricing.
2. Directly priced cosmetics at $1.99-3.99, sold for real money with no intermediate currency and no loot boxes:
   - bloom sets (what Mopes turn into: cherry petals, paper lanterns, fireflies, snow);
   - keeper (tower) skins;
   - canal and gate themes;
   - ASMR sound packs.
3. Prestige cosmetics earned only through skill, following BTD6's Trophy Store: rewards from Flow mode, weekly restriction challenges and boss events.
4. An optional $2.99-4.99 Supporter Pack at launch for players who simply want to pay.
5. Later, only once retention is proven:
   - a free seasonal event track with cosmetic rewards;
   - an optional paid cosmetic track at $3-5;
   - past cosmetics return later, so there is no fear-of-missing-out pressure.

HARD RULES (each backed by the findings)
- No energy, stamina or lives timers. They lock players out of retries at exactly the wrong moment.
- No forced, interstitial or banner ads. One disruptive ad raises churn 6-7%, and 52% of players quit after repeated exposure.
- If a free-tier ad is ever tested, make it a single opt-in rewarded ad at the end of a level only, removed permanently by any purchase.
- Never sell towers, upgrade paths, boosts or starting cash. Kingdom Rush 5's paywalled towers drew backlash, and 'microtransactions in a paid game' is the top cluster in BTD6's negative reviews.
- Never charge for anything that was previously free (BTD6's 2020 Monkey Knowledge backlash).
- No loot boxes, which parents object to. Keep Flow mode and leaderboards pure: no purchased advantages.
- iCloud save from day one, because lost progress is a top complaint in reviews.

PLATFORM ECONOMICS
- Join the App Store Small Business Program for 15% commission from day one.
- Keep StoreKit IAP as the default purchase path.
- A US link-out web shop is an optional later experiment. It is 0% now, Apple has proposed 5% for Small Business Program members, and Apple leadership reportedly wants higher margins, so do not forecast on it.
- Treat Apple Arcade as a possible later upfront deal for an all-inclusive '+' edition, run alongside the paid app, as Balatro and Kingdom Rush 5 do. Do not treat it as the business: payouts are opaque and falling.
- Avoid depending on Netflix, which removed many premium indies in 2025.

DISCOVERY (the biggest risk)
- Release on Steam at the same time as iOS and enter Steam TD Fest in March.
- Market through creators and streamers, as Thronefall and Tangy TD did.
- Aim for App Store editorial features through Apple Design Award-style craft: per-action haptics, a distinctive art style and snappy controls.
- Use portrait screenshots in which frame 1 shows a finger flipping a gate as the coloured stream splits.
- iOS paid installs cost about $1.41 each, so do not rely on paid user acquisition.

WHY PLAYERS RETURN
- 12-15 minute levels that fit a session.
- A daily seeded challenge and a weekly restriction challenge.
- Star and mastery goals on each level.
- A bloom journal to collect, and a garden that visibly grows.
- A steady cadence of new waterways.

EXPECTATIONS
Plan for a modest long tail. After seven years and huge amounts of content, BTD6 earns about $60-106K per Sensor Tower reporting period from paid iOS sales. Do not quote third-party 'market size' figures; they disagree by about 3x.
design_lessons: Keep the surface accessible and the depth underneath: a few towers, each with distinct upgrade forks, soft counters and synergy with other towers. BTD6 is praised for exactly this. Depth per tower matters more than tower count.

Avoid lock-and-key counters. Sending an enemy down the wrong channel should cost efficiency, not guarantee it gets through, so several builds and routing styles can win. This follows Doucet's Defender's Quest lessons and answers BTD6 veterans' complaints about a solved meta.

Maximise planning time and minimise time spent just watching. Give the player a handful of meaningful in-wave choices per wave, each with a visible consequence, and avoid tap-spam. Conduct THIS! was widely called too hard; Anomaly-style planning while paused fixes that.

Keep tapping manageable as waves densify. Make limited gate automation a paid upgrade that competes with towers for money (for example one auto-sort rule per gate, as with Rail Route's sensors), and keep manual override so the twist never disappears.

Make consequences readable:
- floating markers show where enemies got through;
- the loss screen shows which gate decision or tower choice would have stopped them.
This turns failure into a wish to try a different strategy.
Make progress visible: the garden blooms as you play, and an end-of-level picture of the garden gives players something to share, as Mini Motorways players shared their cities.
Win featuring with a distinctive handmade art direction rather than fidelity. Avoid saccharine cuteness so adult strategy players take the game seriously.
Budget simulation cost as well as rendering, so late waves hold their frame rate on older iPhones. BTD6's late-game lag comes from calculations, not graphics.
pain_points_to_solve: TD's 'more watching than doing' problem: little in-wave agency beyond ability buttons.
Long rounds: BTD6 games often run 30+ minutes, CHIMPS runs can take 2+ hours, and 100+ round runs cause burnout.
No way to pause mid-wave and act in BTD6. Pausing and issuing commands should be standard.
Solved meta and repeated builds. The variety exists, but players do not discover it without prompts.
Late-game clutter and slowdown from too many projectiles and entities.
On phones the finger covers the placement spot, and 'one-handed' portrait TD games often need two hands in practice.
Paywalled towers and heroes on top of the purchase price: Kingdom Rush 5 on mobile costs about $48 with everything unlocked, against about $20 on PC.
Microtransactions and currency inside a paid game (the top cluster in BTD6's negative reviews), and charging for things that used to be free.
Energy and stamina systems that lock players out of retrying after a loss.
Forced ads between waves and after matches. Disruptive ads measurably drive churn.
Loot boxes and gambling-style mechanics that parents object to.
Lost progress on reinstall or device change because there is no reliable cloud save.
Buggy paid DLC launches, prices only in US dollars, and paid content released too quickly.
Real-time switching games that feel too hard (Conduct THIS!) and randomness with no undo (Isle of Arrows).
Complexity that confuses younger or newer players, with little guidance on what to try next.
Very large installs (Arknights is about 28GB) and games that need a connection instead of working fully offline.
Poor discoverability for premium indie TD on iOS (Isle of Arrows has 272 ratings against BTD6's roughly 348K).
